n: With no willing heir, Mosiah does something unusual for a king: he asks the people who they want as their next ruler.

f.g: Consulting the people foreshadows the government by “the voice of the people” he is about to propose.

n: The people choose Aaron, one of Mosiah’s sons.
But Aaron has already left for the land of Nephi, and none of Mosiah’s sons wants the throne. Their mission mattered more to them than a crown.

f.w: neither would Aaron take upon him the kingdom

n: So Mosiah sends a written proclamation among the people. What follows (verses 5–32) is his letter proposing a new form of government.

f.g: Putting it in writing let every community read and weigh the same argument.

n: Mosiah addresses the people as brothers, not just subjects, and asks them to think carefully about their wish for a king.
He reminds them that the rightful heir has declined the throne.

f.w: he to whom the kingdom doth rightly belong
f.g: Likely Aaron, whom the people had named in verse 2.

n: Mosiah worries that appointing someone else could backfire: the rightful heir might later change his mind, gather followers, and start a civil war — as Amlici later tries to do anyway.

f.w: draw away a part of this people after him

n: He urges wisdom: they have no right to harm his son, nor any substitute king. A succession fight would hurt everyone.

f.g: Mosiah reasons with his people rather than simply commanding them.

n: If Aaron ever fell back into pride, he might reclaim the throne, leading both himself and the people into sin.

f.g: Empty, worthless pursuits.

n: Mosiah asks them to look ahead and choose whatever will keep the peace.

f.g: Lead to, promote peace.

n: His plan: he will remain king for life, but the nation will shift to elected judges who will judge by the law and God’s commandments.

f.g: The start of the “reign of the judges,” which became the Nephite calendar from Alma 1 onward.

n: Mosiah states a principle: God’s judgments are always just, but human judgments are not. So a system should guard against human failure.

f.w: the judgments of God are always just

n: If kings could always be as righteous as his father Benjamin, monarchy would be best. But that cannot be guaranteed.
Mosiah describes his own reign: he worked with all his strength to teach God’s commandments and keep peace, free of war, theft, and murder.

f.w: labored with all the power and faculties

n: He punished wrongdoing only according to the law handed down from their fathers — not by personal whim.
Because not all people are just, it is unwise to entrust power to a king.

f.g: Not wise or advisable.

n: One wicked king can cause enormous sin and destruction among his people.
Mosiah points to a recent example everyone just heard about: King Noah, whose wickedness led his people into destruction and bondage.
Only God’s intervention, prompted by their sincere repentance, freed Noah’s people.

f.g: Stepping in between; intervention.

n: God freed them because they humbled themselves and cried to him. Mosiah draws a broad lesson: the Lord extends mercy to all who trust him.
A practical problem with kings: removing a wicked one usually requires conflict and bloodshed.

f.g: Remove from the throne.

n: A wicked king surrounds himself with corrupt friends and guards, tears up the righteous laws of his predecessors, and tramples God’s commandments.
He makes laws that suit his wickedness and destroys anyone who resists. In this way an unrighteous king corrupts a whole nation’s sense of right.

f.g: Twist away from what is right.

n: Mosiah does not want his people to suffer such evils.

f.g: Things hateful to God.

n: So he proposes that the people choose judges by their own voice, to judge by laws given through their fathers by the Lord.

f.w: by the voice of this people

n: A key principle: the majority usually chooses right, while a smaller part often wants wrong. So decisions should be made by “the voice of the people.”

f.g: Not pure democracy in the modern sense, but a system of chosen judges accountable to the people.

n: A sober warning: when the majority chooses evil, God’s judgments will follow. This prophecy is fulfilled later in Nephite history.

f.w: the voice of the people doth choose iniquity

n: Checks and balances: a judge who breaks the law can be judged by a higher judge.

f.g: An early appeals system.

n: And if higher judges go wrong, a group of lower judges can judge them — no one stands above the law.

f.g: Accountability runs in both directions.

n: Mosiah commands these changes and that they have no king, so each person will be responsible for his own sins rather than being led into them by a ruler.
Many peoples sin because their kings lead them astray, so that guilt rests on the kings.
Mosiah’s great hope: no more inequality, but a land of liberty where everyone enjoys the same rights — a vision that resonates with later ideals of freedom.
Mosiah wrote much more, describing the burdens of a righteous king — his anxieties for the people and the complaints he received.

f.g: Deep, painful concern.

n: He taught that the burden of government should not rest on one man; every person should share responsibility.

f.w: every man might bear his part

n: He also explained the many disadvantages of living under an unrighteous king.

f.g: Hardships, harms.

n: He listed the evils such kings bring — wars, bloodshed, theft, sexual sin, and more — all contrary to God’s commandments.

f.g: Opposed to, contrary to.
Sexual immorality.

n: Persuaded by his reasoning, the people accepted his words.

f.w: convinced of the truth of his words
f.g: The change came by persuasion, not force.

n: They gave up wanting a king and became eager for everyone to have an equal chance, each willing to answer for his own sins.
The people gathered across the land to vote for judges, rejoicing in their new freedom.

f.g: Gave their votes.

n: Their love for Mosiah grew. He had never sought wealth, never enjoyed bloodshed, and had freed them from bondage — so they honored him above any other man.

f.g: Money or profit, especially gained dishonestly.
A cruel ruler with absolute power.

n: Judges were appointed throughout the land to govern according to the law.

f.g: Compare the judges Moses appointed in Israel.

n: Alma the Younger becomes the first chief judge while also serving as high priest over the church, having received that charge from his father.
Alma governs righteously and the land enjoys continual peace — at least for now.
So begins the reign of the judges over the Nephites — about 91 BC. The book of Alma will count years from this point.
Alma the Elder dies at eighty-two, having faithfully kept God’s commandments.

f.g: He was born about 173 BC, according to this reckoning.

n: Mosiah also dies at sixty-three, after thirty-three years as king — 509 years after Lehi left Jerusalem.

f.g: Counting from 600 BC, this is about 91 BC.

n: Thus ends the line of Nephite kings, and the life of Alma, founder of the church among this people. A new era begins.
